title: Sentence Builder
note: Sentence combining: each step joins one new idea to the sentence as a clause.

steps.idea: She had overslept.
steps.ask: Join it as the reason.
steps.label: Reason clause

joins.t: because she had overslept
although she had overslept
joins.why: Although signals a surprise. Oversleeping isn’t surprising here — it explains why she missed the bus.

joins.t: so she had overslept
joins.why: So introduces a result. Oversleeping came first: it is the cause, not the result.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between the and its noun, bus.

result.t: Maya missed the bus
because she had overslept

steps.note: A reason clause answers why? At the end of the sentence it needs no comma.

steps.idea: Maya lives on the edge of town.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about Maya.
steps.label: Relative clause (who)

joins.t: , who lives on the edge of town,
, which lives on the edge of town,
joins.why: Which is for things. Maya is a person, so use who.

joins.t: , that lives on the edge of town,
joins.why: That can’t introduce extra information between commas. Use who.

gaps.why: A relative clause goes straight after the noun it describes. Here that noun is Maya.

result.t: Maya
, who lives on the edge of town,
missed the bus
because she had overslept

steps.note: Extra information about a person goes straight after the person, between two commas.

steps.idea: She had to run all the way to school.
steps.ask: Join it as the result.
steps.label: Result clause (so)

joins.t: , so she had to run all the way to school
, because she had to run all the way to school
joins.why: Because gives a reason. Running to school didn’t cause anything — it happened because of the missed bus.

joins.t: , although she had to run all the way to school
joins.why: Although signals a contrast, but running is the natural result here, not a surprise.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split the from its noun.

result.t: Maya
, who lives on the edge of town,
missed the bus
because she had overslept
, so she had to run all the way to school

steps.note: A result clause with so follows its cause and takes a comma before so.

steps.idea: His sister could come too.
steps.ask: Join it as the purpose — why two tickets?
steps.label: Purpose clause (so that)

joins.t: so that his sister could come too
in order to his sister could come too
joins.why: In order to is followed by a verb only, with no subject. With a subject, use so that.

joins.t: unless his sister could come too
joins.why: Unless means except if. Leo didn’t buy two tickets on a condition — he bought them for his sister.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split two from tickets.

result.t: Leo bought two tickets
so that his sister could come too

steps.note: So that + subject + could shows purpose: what the action was for.

steps.idea: The tickets cost him a month’s pocket money.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about the tickets.
steps.label: Relative clause (which)

joins.t: , which cost him a month’s pocket money,
, who cost him a month’s pocket money,
joins.why: Who is for people. Tickets are things, so use which.

joins.t: , what cost him a month’s pocket money,
joins.why: What can’t point back to a noun. Use which after a comma.

gaps.why: Which describes the noun just before it. Put it after tickets, not after Leo.

result.t: Leo bought two tickets
, which cost him a month’s pocket money,
so that his sister could come too

steps.note: Extra information about a thing uses which, straight after the thing, between commas.

steps.idea: He heard about the concert.
steps.ask: Join it to say when — put it first.
steps.label: Time clause (as soon as)

joins.t: As soon as he heard about the concert,
Despite he heard about the concert,
joins.why: Despite is followed by a noun or an -ing form, never by a subject and verb.

joins.t: During he heard about the concert,
joins.why: During is followed by a noun: during the concert. It can’t start a clause.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between bought and what he bought.

result.t: As soon as he heard about the concert,
Leo bought two tickets
, which cost him a month’s pocket money,
so that his sister could come too

steps.note: A time clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.

steps.idea: We had trained every day.
steps.ask: Join it as a contrast — put it first.
steps.label: Contrast clause (although)

joins.t: Although we had trained every day,
Because we had trained every day,
joins.why: Training every day doesn’t explain losing — it makes losing surprising. That is a contrast.

joins.t: However we had trained every day,
joins.why: However can’t join two clauses in one sentence. It starts a new sentence: However, …

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between lost and what was lost.

result.t: Although we had trained every day,
our team lost the final

steps.note: Although + clause, then a comma: the main clause says what surprisingly happened.

steps.idea: The final was played on a muddy pitch.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about the final.
steps.label: Relative clause (which)

joins.t: , which was played on a muddy pitch
, where was played on a muddy pitch
joins.why: Where needs its own subject: where we played. Here which is the subject.

joins.t: , that was played on a muddy pitch
joins.why: That can’t introduce extra information after a comma. Use which.

gaps.why: Which describes the noun just before it. The final was muddy, not the training.

result.t: Although we had trained every day,
our team lost the final
, which was played on a muddy pitch

steps.note: Which + extra information, straight after the noun it describes.

steps.idea: Our captain slipped in the last minute.
steps.ask: Join it as the main reason.
steps.label: Reason clause (because)

joins.t: , mainly because our captain slipped in the last minute
, mainly so our captain slipped in the last minute
joins.why: So introduces a result. The slip caused the defeat, so it is the reason.

joins.t: , mainly despite our captain slipped in the last minute
joins.why: Despite can’t be followed by a subject and verb, and a slip isn’t a contrast here.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between had and trained.

result.t: Although we had trained every day,
our team lost the final
, which was played on a muddy pitch
, mainly because our captain slipped in the last minute

steps.note: A reason clause can take a word like mainly or partly in front of because.

base.t: Sofia left her phone on the train

steps.idea: She was getting off in a hurry.
steps.ask: Join it to say when.
steps.label: Time clause (while)

joins.t: while she was getting off in a hurry
during she was getting off in a hurry
joins.why: During is followed by a noun, not a clause. With a subject and verb, use while.

joins.t: whereas she was getting off in a hurry
joins.why: Whereas compares two different facts. This clause says when it happened.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split her from phone.

result.t: Sofia left her phone on the train
while she was getting off in a hurry

steps.note: While + past continuous gives the longer action in the background.

steps.idea: Its screen had just been repaired.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about the phone.
steps.label: Relative clause (whose)

joins.t: , whose screen had just been repaired,
, which screen had just been repaired,
joins.why: For possession — the phone’s screen — use whose, not which.

joins.t: , who’s screen had just been repaired,
joins.why: Who’s means who is. The possessive word is whose.

gaps.why: Whose screen describes the phone, so it goes straight after phone.

result.t: Sofia left her phone
, whose screen had just been repaired,
on the train
while she was getting off in a hurry

steps.note: Whose + noun shows possession, and it can describe things as well as people.

steps.idea: Her mum had warned her to be careful.
steps.ask: Join it as a contrast at the end.
steps.label: Contrast clause (even though)

joins.t: , even though her mum had warned her to be careful
, in spite of her mum had warned her to be careful
joins.why: In spite of is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a subject and verb.

joins.t: , so that her mum had warned her to be careful
joins.why: So that shows purpose. Sofia didn’t lose the phone in order for her mum to warn her.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between left and her phone.

result.t: Sofia left her phone
, whose screen had just been repaired,
on the train
while she was getting off in a hurry
, even though her mum had warned her to be careful

steps.note: Even though is a stronger although: it stresses the surprise.

steps.idea: They had finished their exams.
steps.ask: Join it to say when — put it first.
steps.label: Time clause (after)

joins.t: After they had finished their exams,
Despite they had finished their exams,
joins.why: Despite is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a subject and verb.

joins.t: Unless they had finished their exams,
joins.why: Unless means except if. This clause says when the visit happened, not a condition.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between visited and the museum.

result.t: After they had finished their exams,
the class visited the museum

steps.note: After + past perfect shows which action came first. At the start, add a comma.

steps.idea: They saw a dinosaur skeleton there.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about the museum.
steps.label: Relative clause (where)

joins.t: , where they saw a dinosaur skeleton
, which they saw a dinosaur skeleton
joins.why: Which would need in which here. For a place, use where.

joins.t: , there they saw a dinosaur skeleton
joins.why: There can’t join two clauses. With a comma it makes a run-on sentence. Use where.

gaps.why: Where describes a place. It goes after museum, not after class.

result.t: After they had finished their exams,
the class visited the museum
, where they saw a dinosaur skeleton

steps.note: Where introduces information about a place, with its own subject and verb.

steps.idea: The skeleton was taller than a bus.
steps.ask: Join it to say which skeleton — no commas.
steps.label: Defining clause (that)

joins.t: that was taller than a bus
who was taller than a bus
joins.why: Who is for people. A skeleton is a thing: use that or which.

joins.t: what was taller than a bus
joins.why: What can’t point back to a noun. Use that.

gaps.why: That describes the noun just before it. The skeleton was tall, not the museum.

result.t: After they had finished their exams,
the class visited the museum
, where they saw a dinosaur skeleton
that was taller than a bus

steps.note: A defining clause tells you which one, so it takes no commas.

steps.idea: He was playing a video game.
steps.ask: Join it as the reason.
steps.label: Reason clause (because)

joins.t: because he was playing a video game
although he was playing a video game
joins.why: Although signals a surprise. Playing a game explains the burnt pizza — it isn’t a contrast.

joins.t: so that he was playing a video game
joins.why: So that shows purpose. Dan didn’t burn the pizza in order to play.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split the from pizza.

result.t: Dan burnt the pizza
because he was playing a video game

steps.note: Because + clause gives the reason. No comma is needed at the end.

steps.idea: He had made the pizza from scratch.
steps.ask: Join it to say which pizza — no commas.
steps.label: Defining clause (that)

joins.t: that he had made from scratch
who he had made from scratch
joins.why: Who is for people. A pizza is a thing, so use that.

joins.t: what he had made from scratch
joins.why: What can’t point back to a noun. Use that.

gaps.why: That describes the noun just before it: the pizza, not Dan.

result.t: Dan burnt the pizza
that he had made from scratch
because he was playing a video game

steps.note: In that he had made, the pizza is the object, so there is no second it.

steps.idea: His dad had set a timer.
steps.ask: Join it as a contrast — put it first.
steps.label: Contrast clause (even though)

joins.t: Even though his dad had set a timer,
Even his dad had set a timer,
joins.why: Even on its own can’t join two clauses. Use even though.

joins.t: In spite of his dad had set a timer,
joins.why: In spite of is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a subject and verb.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split the from pizza.

result.t: Even though his dad had set a timer,
Dan burnt the pizza
that he had made from scratch
because he was playing a video game

steps.note: Even though at the start sets up the surprise before the main clause.

steps.idea: Aisha had just moved from Lisbon.
steps.ask: Join it as extra information about Aisha.
steps.label: Relative clause (who)

joins.t: , who had just moved from Lisbon,
, which had just moved from Lisbon,
joins.why: Which is for things. Aisha is a person, so use who.

joins.t: , she had just moved from Lisbon,
joins.why: She starts a new clause with nothing to join it. Use who.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split our from class.

result.t: Aisha
, who had just moved from Lisbon,
joined our class

steps.note: Who + extra information, straight after the person, between commas.

steps.idea: She felt nervous on her first day.
steps.ask: Join it at the start, with an -ing form.
steps.label: Participle clause (-ing)

joins.t: Feeling nervous on her first day,
Felt nervous on her first day,
joins.why: A past verb with no subject can’t open the sentence. Use the -ing form.

joins.t: To feel nervous on her first day,
joins.why: To + verb shows purpose. She didn’t join the class in order to feel nervous.

gaps.why: A clause can’t come between joined and our class.

result.t: Feeling nervous on her first day,
Aisha
, who had just moved from Lisbon,
joined our class

steps.note: An -ing clause at the start must describe the subject that follows it: Aisha.

steps.idea: Within a week she had made three friends.
steps.ask: Join it as a contrast at the end.
steps.label: Contrast clause (but)

joins.t: , but within a week she had made three friends
, because within a week she had made three friends
joins.why: Because gives a reason. Making friends didn’t cause her to join — it happened afterwards, despite her nerves.

joins.t: , so that within a week she had made three friends
joins.why: So that shows purpose. The friends are a surprise, not the purpose.

gaps.why: The contrast answers the whole sentence, so it goes at the end.

result.t: Feeling nervous on her first day,
Aisha
, who had just moved from Lisbon,
joined our class
, but within a week she had made three friends

steps.note: But joins two main clauses. Put a comma before it.

steps.idea: They worry about screen time.
steps.ask: Join it as the reason.
steps.label: Reason clause (because)

joins.t: because they worry about screen time
despite they worry about screen time
joins.why: Despite can’t be followed by a subject and verb, and worry is the reason, not a contrast.

joins.t: so they worry about screen time
joins.why: So introduces a result. The worry comes first: it is the reason for the ban.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split video from games.

result.t: Many parents ban video games
because they worry about screen time

steps.note: Because + clause: the reason, with no comma at the end of the sentence.

steps.idea: These parents rarely play games themselves.
steps.ask: Join it to say which parents — no commas.
steps.label: Defining clause (who)

joins.t: who rarely play games themselves
which rarely play games themselves
joins.why: Which is for things. Parents are people, so use who.

joins.t: whose rarely play games themselves
joins.why: Whose needs a noun after it, like whose children. Here use who.

gaps.why: Who describes the noun just before it. It goes after parents.

result.t: Many parents
who rarely play games themselves
ban video games
because they worry about screen time

steps.note: A defining clause tells you which parents, so no commas.

steps.idea: Some games can improve problem-solving skills.
steps.ask: Join it as a contrast — put it first.
steps.label: Contrast clause (although)

joins.t: Although some games can improve problem-solving skills,
Despite some games can improve problem-solving skills,
joins.why: Despite is followed by a noun or -ing form: despite the benefits.

joins.t: Because some games can improve problem-solving skills,
joins.why: Better skills don’t explain a ban — they make the ban surprising. That is a contrast.

gaps.why: A clause can’t split video from games.

result.t: Although some games can improve problem-solving skills,
many parents
who rarely play games themselves
ban video games
because they worry about screen time

steps.note: This is an essay sentence: contrast, main claim, who, and a reason in one line.
